title: Factory-Built One-Off Ford Mustang V-10 Roars to Life After Years of Sitting
summary: There’s an unusual, New Edge Mustang-based prototype sitting in Ford’s heritage collection. body_markdown:
There’s an unusual,[New Edge Mustang](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/why-on-earth-are-sn95-mustangs-slept-on-by-enthusiasts/) -based prototype sitting in Ford’s heritage collection. It looks like a regular production car, but popping the hood reveals a V-10 that remained at the prototype stage. After gathering dust for years, the one-of-one Ford Mustang V-10 was resurrected in-house and put on a dyno by some of the same people who built it.


Our own Grace Jarvis[wrote about the one-off Mustang V-10](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/8-notable-vehicles-from-fords-new-u-s-heritage-collection/) after visiting Ford’s heritage collection in March 2025. She explained that the car was built by a small team of engineers who wanted to prove to management that the Blue Oval could give[the Dodge Viper](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/7-dodge-viper-facts-you-may-not-know-from-the-men-who-built-it/) and the Chevrolet Corvette a run for their money. Instead of using the V-10 that powered the F-Series Super Duty of the era, the team grafted a pair of additional cylinders onto the Mustang’s modular 4.6-liter V-8 block to create a 5.8-liter 10-cylinder.


The engine was developed as a proposal for[the then-upcoming GT](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2006-ford-gt-heritage-edition-for-sale-auction/) , but prototypes weren’t available yet, so it was tested in a leftover 1999 Mustang test car that Ford had used to develop the Cobra R. While the engine was dauntingly experimental, it let the Mustang cover a quarter mile in 12.28 seconds at 117 mph, figures that made it quicker than the then-new supercharged 2003 Cobra.


Ford decided not to move forward with the V-10 project, and the GT made its debut in 2005 with a 5.4-liter V-8 supercharged to 550 horsepower. While test mules often end up scrapped, the 10-cylinder Mustang survived. It was occasionally moved around between storage facilities, according to Ford, and it sometimes came close to getting sent to the crusher, but it was special enough that someone always argued in favor of saving it. The brand began the difficult process of bringing it back to life earlier in 2026.

Starting an engine that hasn’t been fired up in years is rarely a straightforward process, but this V-10 isn’t just any engine. It’s a one-off built with a blend of Ford parts, aftermarket parts, and purpose-built parts. If something breaks, there’s a chance you’ll need to machine a replacement. Ford notes that the electronics had to be overhauled, too. Some of the people who worked on the car in the 2000s helped bring it back to life. The engine started for the first time in years in August 2026, and the car was put on a dyno.


The result is a mighty 510 horsepower at the wheels. Factor in drivetrain loss, and the V-10 likely makes well north of 550 horsepower at the crank. The numbers only tell part of the story;[The sound](https://www.fromtheroad.ford.com/us/en/articles/2026/ford-v10-mustang-heritage-fleet-revival) is amazing. Matt Korczyk, the manager of Ford’s heritage fleet, summed it up well: “The V-10 has a sound all of its own. It’s raw. Mechanical. It doesn’t sound like anything we’d build today.”


While hearing the V-10 roar for the first time in years was rewarding, Korczyk said that the best part of the project was bringing together the people who originally worked on the car. “Preserving a vehicle isn’t really about the vehicle. The car is just the vessel. What you’re really preserving are the stories. The people. The ideas. The late nights. The ‘hey, what if we tried this?’ moments.”
